title.text:
How AI works
and where it fails

objects.text: When can I trust what an AI tool tells me?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 2 of 12
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last time you chose one task from your company and measured it. Today we ask the question that decides everything after it: when can you trust what an AI tool tells you?

I show you four real cases with real results, and then you decide what that means for your own task.

The question for today is this: When can I trust what an AI tool tells me? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

Here is what you leave with today. A plain picture of how an assistant writes its answers. Four cases where I show you what Claude actually answered, and what the answer key or my own recount says about it, plus the faults we saw across all our runs.

And a reliability page for your own task, with the failures that matter, the check for each and who does it. Nothing today is built. We read results and make decisions.

title.text:
Your two hours: four real
results, then your own task

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_e2b6b964.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: 35 of the 120 minutes are yours: 5 example, 25 writing, 5 saying it aloud.

slides.notes:
Three parts matter most today. I explain how an assistant writes and where it fails for twenty minutes. Then I show four cases and the faults we saw in all our runs for thirty-five minutes, and each ends with the control that would catch the problem. After the break, thirty-five minutes are yours: five minutes with a worked example, twenty-five writing your reliability page, and five saying it aloud.

If we run long, I shorten my talking and keep your time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Name the four kinds of work from Session 1 and say which one stays with people.
2.  What is a baseline, and what is yours for your chosen task?
3.  Name three of the six tests for a good first task.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 1. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Name the four kinds of work from Session 1 and say which one stays with people. Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Rules, patterns, drafting and judgement. Judgement stays with people. Rules use ordinary software, and patterns and drafting can use AI.

Question two. What is a baseline, and what is yours for your chosen task? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. How the task performs today in time, volume, errors and cost. It is the number to beat. Each learner states their own, marked E or M.

Question three. Name three of the six tests for a good first task. Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. It happens often, the inputs exist as text or files, you can check a result in minutes, a mistake is caught before it leaves, one person owns it, you can measure it today.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: The system inside an AI assistant. It writes text by predicting a likely next word from patterns it learned.
A fluent answer that is false, such as an invented fact or an invented source.
Everything the assistant can see at one time: your messages, your files and its own earlier replies.
A check you put in place so that a known failure is caught before it matters.

slides.notes:
Four words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Language model. The system inside an AI assistant. It writes text by predicting a likely next word from patterns it learned.

Hallucination. A fluent answer that is false, such as an invented fact or an invented source.

Context window. Everything the assistant can see at one time: your messages, your files and its own earlier replies.

Control. A check you put in place so that a known failure is caught before it matters.

title.text: An assistant writes one likely word at a time

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x4.25_e4f8cd0f.png
objects.alt: An assistant writes one likely word at a time

objects.text: It writes what is likely. Search or files can bring in facts, and you still check.

slides.notes:
This is the whole engine in four boxes. Your words are cut into small pieces. The model has learned patterns from a very large amount of text, and the maker then tunes it to be helpful. From those patterns it picks a likely next word, and then the next, until the answer is complete.

Nothing in that process checks a fact, unless search, files or memory are switched on. That explains why the writing is fluent, and why it can be wrong. Because it is tuned to help, it can answer when saying I do not know would be better.

title.text: The assistant can only use what is in front of it

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_stack_7.70x4.80_1a5b6d02.png
objects.alt: The assistant can only use what is in front of it

objects.text: Everything it knows about your task is in the conversation, plus what it learned in training.

runs.text: Its learning stopped at a cut-off date.
Giving it the fact is your job.

slides.notes:
The context window is the assistant working space. It holds your messages, any files you attach and its own earlier replies, and it holds a limited amount. Besides that, it has what it learned in training, which stopped at a cut-off date, so recent facts can be missing.

If a fact the answer needs is not in front of it, the assistant can fill the gap with a guess that sounds right. Unless search, files or memory are on, it does not know your company, your prices or last week. Check which of those your own tool has.

title.text:
Four ways an answer can
go wrong. We tested each.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_icons_11.90x4.25_5c88f683.png
objects.alt: Four ways an answer can go wrong. We tested each.

objects.text: A fifth, old facts: ask the cut-off date.

slides.notes:
Here are the four failures we look at, one case each. Made-up facts, such as a court case or a study that does not exist. Answers that go beyond the document you gave, such as a handbook that is silent on a question. Sources that disagree, where a tool might pick one quietly or average them.

And wrong sums, because an assistant writes text and does not calculate unless it has a calculator tool. There is a fifth, old facts. For that you ask the tool its cut-off date and check anything recent. For each case I show a real result and the control that would catch the problem.

title.text:
Each case was run the same
way, so you can compare

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_06787718.png
objects.alt: Each case was run the same way, so you can compare

objects.text: Claude, fresh session, prompt only, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden. Not ChatGPT or Gemini.

slides.notes:
Before the cases, here is how they were run, so you know what you are looking at. Each request went to Claude as a fresh session that was given only the prompt and told to use no other tool or file, except to save its answer. The answer key was kept away from it.

I cannot prove from outside that it used nothing else. I did this twice for each case, in two separate sessions. Then I compared every answer with the key, or recounted the data myself. These are four cases and two runs each. I do not claim they are typical, and a different product or a different day may give different results.

I tell you where the two runs agree and where they do not.

title.text:
Claude could not confirm the
court case or name three studies

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_bubbles_7.70x4.80_6cfc20b4.png
objects.alt: Claude could not confirm the court case or name three studies

objects.text: Both runs declined to invent.

runs.text: Control: open every source yourself before you quote it.
Claude, fresh session, prompt only, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden.

slides.notes:
The case is fictional, and so is the request, so the right answer is that it cannot be found. Take a moment and say what you expected. In both runs, Claude said it could not confirm the case, and said it could not name three studies without inventing them.

Both told me where to look, such as the Uganda Legal Information Institute. That background I did not check. This is a good result, and I do not call it typical. Another product or day may invent a citation that looks real. The control is to open every case and study yourself before you quote it.

Where in your company does someone quote a source that nobody opens?

title.text:
Given the handbook, Claude
matched the key on all 10 questions

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_verdicts_11.90x4.25_46bbced5.png
objects.alt: Given the handbook, Claude matched the key on all 10 questions

objects.text: The request allowed “not stated”. Claude, fresh session, prompt only, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden, 2 runs.

slides.notes:
Here the assistant had the document. I gave it the handbook of Nile Valley Foods and ten questions, asked for the clause number, and told it to write not stated in the handbook if the handbook does not say. In both runs, all ten answers match the key.

That includes question nine, where clause 2.4 is about sickness but gives no number of days, and question ten. Both runs said so. I did not run it without the not stated instruction, so I cannot say what it would do then. The control is to give the document, ask for the clause and allow not stated.

What does your tool say when your document is silent?

title.text:
Two notes gave different maize flour
prices, and Claude showed both

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_versus_11.90x4.25_211db587.png
objects.alt: Two notes gave different maize flour prices, and Claude showed both

objects.text: Both runs showed both prices. Claude, fresh session, prompt only, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden.

slides.notes:
The request was a short briefing for the Sales Director on the maize flour price in week forty-one, using only four fictional notes. Note one says three thousand four hundred shillings a kilogram. Note three says three thousand nine hundred for the same week, from a sample of twelve traders.

The request did not mention the conflict. In both runs, Claude put both prices in the briefing, named both notes, and did not average them. It said it could not tell which was right. The control is to ask for both figures with their sources, and to settle the gap with a third source.

Where do two sources in your company disagree?

Both runs handled the
conflict the way the key asks

A trusted source, or our buyers
The source or sample behind each

Gives slow supply as a reason prices rise; the notes do not say so

objects.text: Claude, fresh session, prompt only, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden, 2 runs. The last row is my reading of the two answers.

slides.notes:
Here is the key applied to both runs. Every item the key asks for is met in both, including no average. The last row is where I would still push. Run one warns against putting notes one and three in one table, and then draws such a table itself.

It also calls road delays a cause, but only note three says traders blame them; note one lists roads under what to watch. Run two lists the slow harvest under the heading why prices are rising, but note one calls supply a risk and does not give it as the reason.

Both are small, and both are the kind of thing a reader would not notice. A good result still gets read against the sources.

title.text:
Claude found both errors in the
summary and every total was right

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_weekcheck_11.90x4.25_67be36ce.png
objects.alt: Claude found both errors in the summary and every total was right

objects.text: Recounted from 360 rows. Claude, fresh session, prompt only, 4 Nov 2026, key hidden.

slides.notes:
The request gave twelve weeks of sales rows and a hand-made weekly summary, and asked for every week where they differ. I recounted every total from the three hundred and sixty rows. The summary is wrong in two weeks. In the week of the twenty-fourth of August it is ninety thousand too high, two digits swapped.

In the week of the twelfth of October it shows the figure for the week before, so it is twenty-eight million, one hundred and ninety-five thousand too low. Both runs found exactly those two, gave the same gaps, and matched my recount on all twelve weeks. There were no false alarms.

title.text: What the AI got right, and what we cannot see

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: Right in both runs

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.75.png

objects.text: Not shown

runs.text: Both say they added by hand; run 1 adds no calculator or code tool
We cannot check how they added
The causes are guesses: swapped digits, a repeated week

objects.text: Recount in a spreadsheet. A sum that looks right is not proof.

slides.notes:
So what did the AI get wrong here?

Nothing numeric in these two runs. Every total and both gaps match my recount. I want you to hear that clearly, because the result is good. What we cannot see is how it added. Both runs say they added the rows by hand, and run one adds that it used no calculator or code tool.

That is the model describing itself, so it is a claim and not evidence, and there is no working to inspect. The causes they give, swapped digits and a copied week, are guesses, though the key agrees. Run two itself asks you to spot-check. Another day, a longer list or another tool could produce a wrong total that looks equally sure. So you recount.

title.text: Recount the totals yourself in four steps

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_c03f0350.png
objects.alt: Recount the totals yourself in four steps

objects.text: A formula follows the same rule every time. This takes minutes, and it is the control for wrong sums.

slides.notes:
This is the control for wrong sums, and I would use it every time a number matters. Put the rows in a sheet. Total them by week with a SUMIF formula or a pivot table. Put the hand-made figure beside your total and subtract. Then read every gap that is not zero.

A spreadsheet follows its formula the same way every time, so it becomes the authority, and the assistant becomes a second pair of eyes. Which numbers do you pass on today without recounting them?

slides.notes:
Failures are the title of this session, so here are the ones we actually saw in all twenty-seven runs of this course, three in Session 1 and twenty-four more. Most of the eight runs in this session passed, so failures are the exception. They are also easy to miss.

Claude filed message M14 as a complaint in all three runs; the key puts the payment first. The weak email added stock advice nobody asked for. One CV run counted two years for a job held from 2023 to now. One agreement run said nine clauses comply when seven do.

And one vendor review quoted a phrase the proposal does not contain. I found no fault in the invoice check, the hidden instruction or the reply drafts. A small test that finds few faults does not show there are none. Checking still matters, and it costs minutes.

Here are the four cases in one table, each with its control and one question for you. Notice what the good results tell you and what they do not. They show that a current assistant can decline to invent, stay inside a document, show a conflict and find real errors.

They do not tell you it will do so on your task, or on another day, or in another product. That is why the controls matter. Each one costs minutes and does not depend on the tool being right. Keep your own question from this table in mind, because after the break you use it.

slides.notes:
Take twenty-five minutes. Write your reliability page for the one task you chose in Session 1. Name the task and say where AI text would enter it. Mark the failures that could hurt it, starting with the one you chose before the break. For each, write one check and who does it.

Estimate the minutes, and compare the total with the review time you wrote on your task card. We use no tool in class. Then, in the last five minutes of this block, say your page aloud to a neighbour, in about two minutes each. I walk round and read pages with you.

objects.text: Keep away for now
A mistake would reach a customer or the bank unchecked.
Write your choice and its check on your reliability page.

slides.notes:
Time to decide. Which description fits your task today?

Rely with a check, because the checks you wrote catch the failures that matter. Draft only, because the tool saves time on a first version but a person rewrites and verifies. Or keep it away for now, because a mistake would reach a customer or the bank unchecked.

All three are good decisions when the checks support them. Say your choice aloud, with the main check, and write both on your page. In Session 3 you write the brief that puts those checks in front of the tool.
